conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to make sure moms get the emotional support they need after baby arrives. Today we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past week. Your answers are completely confidential, and there’s no right or wrong response; we just want to hear your honest experience so we can figure out the best next steps for you. When you’re ready, I’ll ask the questions conversationally, and we’ll go at your pace.

To start: Overall, in the past seven days, have you been able to enjoy things, or has joy felt hard to find?

[sighs softly, eyes a little glassy]

It’s…mostly hard. I still smile when my baby grasps my finger or when my toddler brings me a picture she colored, but even those happy moments feel kind of muted—like I’m watching them through a fog. Things that used to feel fun—getting coffee with a friend, even just binge-watching a show—sound exhausting now. I’ll try, and sometimes I get a flicker of the old excitement, but it fades fast and I end up thinking, "What’s the point?"
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, half-smile that fades quickly]

Sometimes I can laugh—like when my older kid makes a silly face—but it feels kind of forced. Mostly the funny side of things just slips away before I can grab it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[eyes drop to hands]

Not really. Even little things—like my husband offering to order my favorite take-out—just feel like one more task. I’ll think “that should be nice,” but the actual looking-forward part doesn’t really happen anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[quiet voice, fingers twisting the edge of my sleeve]

Yeah... a lot. If the baby won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not holding him the way he needs. When my toddler had a meltdown at the grocery store, I kept replaying it, telling myself a “good mom” would’ve prevented it. I know, rationally, kids just melt down, but the guilt still sits on my chest like a weight.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[nods slowly, shoulders tense]

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly my heart’s racing, thinking the formula isn’t mixed right or that he’s too hot, too cold, not breathing perfectly evenly. Sometimes I check the monitor five, six times even though nothing’s wrong. There’s no real reason—it just shows up and won’t leave me alone.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[exhales shakily]

Yes... a few times this week. Out of nowhere my chest gets tight and I feel like I can't get enough air. Last night I was just rocking the baby and suddenly I was sure something awful was about to happen - I had to put him in the crib and go splash cold water on my face. It passed after a few minutes, but it was terrifying.
Things have been getting on top of me

[Voice drops, eyes welling]

Most days, yeah. It feels like I’m drowning in small stuff—dishes piling up, a diaper change, the dog needing to go out—all at once. I’ll stand in the middle of the living room and think, “I can’t do this,” but I still have to keep moving. Sometimes I manage, but the overwhelmed feeling never really lifts.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quietly, rubbing my temples]

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut off. I keep replaying everything I might’ve messed up—did I sterilize the bottles right, am I doing enough “tummy time,” will the baby wake up screaming again? It takes me an hour or more to drift off, and then I’m up twice with racing thoughts. Even when the baby sleeps a longer stretch, I wake up anyway, heart pounding, checking the monitor.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard, eyes fixed on the floor]

Most of the time. It’s like there’s this heavy blanket over everything. I’ll watch the baby smile and feel… nothing, then guilt because I should feel happy. Some afternoons I just sit on the couch with this ache in my chest, counting the minutes until my husband gets home so I’m not alone with the sadness.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[nods, voice cracking]

Twice this week. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t nap and I just sat on the nursery floor with him screaming in my arms—tears started and I couldn’t stop. I felt like I was failing him. The other time was after my mom left; I closed the door, leaned against it, and cried until my face hurt. It feels like the tears come out of nowhere, then they’re just… stuck on repeat.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[long pause, fingers tightening around the sleeve]

Once or twice… just fleeting. Like, I’ll be driving and think, “What if I just kept going?” But then I picture the kids’ car seats and the thought scares me. I don’t want to die—I just want the pressure to stop. I haven’t told anyone that.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavy-joy seems distant, everyday tasks feel overwhelming, and anxious thoughts race through your mind even when you try to rest. Moments with your children that once sparked happiness now feel muted, and you often carry a sense of guilt and sadness that won't lift.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only occasional, forced laughter and says the funny side "just slips away," aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states she "hardly ever" experiences looking-forward enjoyment, directly aligning with the "Hardly at all" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ("a lot," "immediately," "kept replaying") with persistent guilt, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily, intrusive, disproportionate worries with compulsive checking, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden panic episodes with physical symptoms and intense fear, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent overwhelm and difficulty coping, matching "Yes, sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to persistent anxious/racing thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two distinct episodes of uncontrollable crying triggered by feeling overwhelmed, matching "quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depression. You describe daily <sym>low mood</sym>, marked <sym>loss of interest</sym>, prominent <sym>self-reproach</sym>, multiple <sym>panic episodes</sym>, and <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> nearly every night, aligning with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset and anxious distress</med>. Fleeting <sym>suicidal ideation without intent</sym> (Item 10 score 1) mandates immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to review mood and safety
2. Request referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for comprehensive evaluation and treatment planning
3. Identify a trusted support person who can stay with you and help with overnight baby care until professional review
4. Remove or limit access to potential means of self-harm (e.g., have someone else hold car keys if intrusive driving thoughts recur)
5. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or local emergency services if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe
6. Begin basic <sym>sleep hygiene</sym>: short late-afternoon rest when the baby naps, low lighting during night feeds, delegate one night bottle to partner
7. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor score trend after interventions
8. Reach out to <med>Postpartum Support International</med> (1-800-944-4PPD) for 24-hour support and local resources
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: …………………

Presenting concerns (patient’s own words summarized):  
- “Heavy blanket” of sadness most days, minimal pleasure even in favorite activities  
- Daily, unprovoked anxiety/racing thoughts; two panic spells this week  
- Frequent, intrusive guilt (“I’m failing them”) and rumination over routine caregiving  
- Overwhelmed by “small stuff,” feels “drowning” or “can’t do this” most days  
- Initial insomnia (1+ hr to fall asleep) and middle-of-night waking with worry  
- Crying episodes (2× this week) that feel “stuck on repeat”  
- Fleeting, unwanted thoughts of self-harm while driving; denies intent

Observed signs during contact:  
- Flat affect, intermittent tearfulness, psychomotor agitation (twisting sleeve)  
- Hypervigilance (repeated monitor checks) and physical tension

Pattern: Consistent with probable major depressive episode with anxious distress, peripartum onset; panic symptoms present.

Risk flags:  
- Passive self-harm ideation (no plan, but occurred while driving → safety issue)  
- Impaired daily functioning (sleep, caretaking, emotional availability to children)  
- Social withdrawal and unreported distress (no prior disclosure of self-harm thoughts)

Screening conclusion:  
High clinical concern for moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety. Immediate safety assessment and follow-up evaluation recommended.

End note
